title: Mucus in Urine: What It Means on a Urinalysis and When It Matters
summary: Mucus in urine is usually normal in small or moderate amounts. Learn what a large amount can mean, how to read it with infection signs, and what to do next.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Mucus in urine is usually normal in small or moderate amounts. A large amount can be a sign of a urinary tract infection (UTI) or another condition, and it means more tests are needed to find the cause** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]. Mucus is a thick, slippery fluid that coats and moistens the urinary tract, so a little of it ends up in every urine sample \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \].


The mucus line rarely decides anything on its own. Its meaning depends on who gave the sample, how it was collected, what else the same urinalysis shows, and whether you have symptoms. In women, mucus in a sample can come from the vagina or cervix rather than the bladder \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24627718/) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \]. After surgery that rebuilds the urinary tract from a piece of intestine, mucus is an expected, ongoing finding \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15290207/) \]\[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11342892/) \].


## What mucus in urine is


**Urine mucus comes mainly from the mucus that lines and protects the urinary tract, and in women it can also come from vaginal or cervical mucus picked up during collection** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]\[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24627718/) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \]. A urinalysis looks for it during the microscopic part of the exam, along with cells, crystals and casts \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \].


Normal urine also carries a protein that most reports never mention: **uromodulin** , also called Tamm-Horsfall protein. It is made only by the cells lining one segment of the kidney tubules, the thick ascending limb and the early distal tubule \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38211973/) \]. It is the most abundant protein in the urine of healthy people, more than half of the total, and it forms long polymers in normal urine \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38211973/) \]. It is also the main building block of hyaline casts \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38211973/) \]\[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


Neither finding is unusual on its own. Mucous threads are often present in normal urine \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41568143/) \], and uromodulin is in everyone’s urine \[[7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38211973/) \].


## How labs report mucus in urine


**Labs report mucus by amount or presence from the microscopic exam, not as a measured number** \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003579.htm) \]. On a Mito report, mucus appears as its own line, Urine Mucus, separate from the cast and crystal lines.


MedlinePlus describes the usual reading this way \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]:


- **A small or moderate amount** is the usual normal result.
- **A large amount** may be a sign of a medical condition and usually leads to more tests to find out why.


If your report uses words such as rare, few, moderate or many, read them against that guidance. Rare or few is at the expected end. Many is the result that calls for a look at the rest of the report.


## Mucus threads vs hyaline casts


**Mucus threads and hyaline casts can look alike under the microscope, but they form in different places and mean different things.** Automated urine analyzers are built specifically to tell hyaline casts apart from mucous threads \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41568143/) \].


Finding Where it forms What it usually means


Mucus threads The lining of the urinary tract, or the genital area during collection \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]\[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24627718/) \] Often present in normal urine. Larger amounts are associated with inflammation or irritation of the urinary tract \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]\[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41568143/) \]


[Hyaline casts](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-casts) Inside the kidney tubules, as a gel of uromodulin that keeps the tube’s cylindrical shape \[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26079824/) \] May be a normal finding, including with fever or dehydration, or may occur with kidney disease \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26079824/) \]\[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


Red or white blood cell casts Inside the kidney tubules, with cells trapped in the protein \[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \] Point to the kidney rather than the bladder. Red and white blood cell casts confirm glomerular disease \[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]\[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


The difference is location. Casts localize a problem to the kidney \[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \]. Mucus does not. Crystals are a separate finding again; see[urine crystals](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-crystals) .


## Mucus in urine in females


**In women, extra mucus in a urine sample can come from vaginal or cervical mucus picked up during collection.** Glands in the cervix and the walls of the vagina normally make clear mucus, and the amount changes through the menstrual cycle \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \]. Ovulation, pregnancy and sexual arousal all increase normal vaginal discharge \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \].


Vaginal discharge and mucus in a sample can also lead to misreading other urinalysis results, such as leukocyte esterase \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24627718/) \].


Two clues on the same report suggest contamination:


- **Many squamous epithelial cells.** These skin-type cells line the outer urethra and the vulva. More than five per high-power field suggests the sample was contaminated \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. On a Mito report this is[epithelial cells, non-renal](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-epithelial-cells-non-renal) .
- **Bacteria.** Bacteria appear with both contamination and infection, so a culture is needed to identify a dominant species \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


**White mucus or white threads you see in the toilet** may also come from vaginal discharge. Normal vaginal secretions can turn white or yellow when exposed to air \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \]. A change in the amount, color, smell or consistency of discharge, or itching, can point to a vaginal infection rather than a urinary one \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \].


## Mucus in urine in males


**Vaginal and cervical mucus cannot explain a man’s result, so the other causes of a large amount of mucus matter more.** The causes on the MedlinePlus list apply to everyone: a UTI, a sexually transmitted infection, kidney stones, irritable bowel syndrome or bladder cancer \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \].


In men, the clean-catch method still matters. It means cleaning the head of the penis, pulling back the foreskin if present, and collecting from the middle of the stream \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]. The presence of bacteria in a properly collected male sample suggests infection, and a culture should be obtained \[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


## When mucus is expected: urinary diversion


**After bladder surgery that uses a segment of intestine, mucus in the urine is an expected, ongoing finding.** This includes an ileal conduit (a urostomy) and a neobladder or other bladder reconstruction \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15290207/) \]\[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11342892/) \].


The intestinal segment keeps doing what intestine does: it makes mucus \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15290207/) \]. Problems from heavy mucus production do not tend to fade with time \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15290207/) \]. In a trial of 43 people with an ileal conduit or a bladder reconstruction, 67% reported that their mucus production had not decreased over time \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11342892/) \]. The same trial found that three drugs tested to reduce mucus worked no better than placebo \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11342892/) \].


If you have had one of these operations, a lot of mucus on a urinalysis is expected after the surgery. Infection signs on the rest of the report, and symptoms, matter more than the mucus line itself.


## When mucus in urine matters: signs of infection


**Mucus matters most when it sits next to signs of infection on the same urinalysis.** A UTI is the first cause MedlinePlus lists for a large amount of mucus \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]. The lines below carry more weight than mucus does.


Report line What a positive result adds


[Nitrite](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-nitrite) Bacteria that convert nitrate to nitrite. With symptoms, a positive nitrite strongly suggests a UTI \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Leukocyte esterase](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-leukocytes) An enzyme from white blood cells, a sign of inflammation or infection, including sexually transmitted infections \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[White blood cells](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-white-blood-cells) More than 5 per high-power field is consistent with a UTI in someone with symptoms \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Bacteria](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-bacteria) Seen with both infection and contamination, so a culture is needed \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


[Squamous epithelial cells](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/urine-epithelial-cells-non-renal) More than 5 per high-power field suggests contamination, which makes the lines above less reliable \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]


For how to read these lines together, including a negative nitrite with positive leukocytes, see[what nitrites in urine mean](https://mitohealth.com/blog/nitrites-in-urine) .


Common UTI symptoms include pain or burning when urinating, a strong need to urinate often, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. Mucus with these symptoms points toward a culture. Mucus without symptoms and without other infection signs usually does not.


**Bacteria without symptoms are not always a problem.** Asymptomatic bacteriuria means bacteria in the urine with no urinary symptoms \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \]. The 2019 Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guideline recommends screening for and treating it only in pregnancy and before invasive urologic procedures \[[14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \].


## Other causes of a large amount of mucus


Besides a UTI, MedlinePlus lists these possible causes of a large amount of mucus in urine \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]:


- a sexually transmitted infection;
- kidney stones;
- irritable bowel syndrome;
- bladder cancer.


Mucous threads are also associated with inflammation or irritation of the urinary tract more generally \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41568143/) \]. The list is a starting point for more tests, not a ranking of likelihood. The bladder cancer known to produce mucus, primary mucinous adenocarcinoma, is an extremely rare type, though some people with it have mucus in the urine as their only sign \[[15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29204001/) \]. The usual next step after a large amount of mucus is further testing to find the cause \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \].


For blood on the same report, see[what blood in urine test results mean](https://mitohealth.com/blog/blood-in-urine-test-results) . For persistent bubbles, see[what foamy urine can mean](https://mitohealth.com/blog/foamy-urine) .


## Mucus in urine during pregnancy


**Pregnancy increases normal vaginal discharge, and that extra mucus can end up in a urine sample** \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24627718/) \]\[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003158.htm) \]. Careful clean-catch collection helps keep it out of the sample \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]\[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].


Pregnancy is also the main situation where bacteria in the urine are screened for and treated even without symptoms \[[14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]. A urine culture is the test used to diagnose asymptomatic bacteriuria \[[13](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000520.htm) \]. So mucus in pregnancy should go to your prenatal clinician together with the infection lines on the report. Pregnant people with a UTI and a fever, or who feel ill, may need hospital care \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].


## What to do after a mucus in urine result


1. **Look at the amount.** A small or moderate amount is usually normal. A large amount calls for the next steps \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \].
2. **Read the other lines on the same report.** Nitrite, leukocyte esterase, white blood cells and bacteria point to infection. Many squamous epithelial cells point to contamination \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \].
3. **Repeat a clean-catch sample when the result is unclear.** Wash your hands, clean the genital area, start urinating into the toilet, then collect the middle of the stream in the container \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \]. If many squamous cells suggest contamination, a repeat clean-catch sample gives a more reliable reading \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. Tell the lab or your provider if you are having your period \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \].
4. **Get a urine culture when an infection is suspected.** A culture is recommended when UTI symptoms are present \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2022/0700/office-based-urinalysis.html) \]. It shows which bacteria, if any, are growing, and results take 24 to 48 hours \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003751.htm) \].
5. **Bring a persistent large amount to your doctor.** A large amount of mucus that keeps returning on repeat samples is the situation where more tests to find the cause make sense \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/mucus-in-urine/) \].


Delays matter too. Urine that waits more than two hours before it is examined often gives unreliable results, so samples that cannot be examined promptly should be refrigerated \[[8](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2005/0315/p1153.html) \].


The **[Urinalysis, Routine Test](https://mitohealth.com/products/urinalysis-routine)** includes the dipstick and the microscopic exam of the urine sediment, so one sample covers the infection lines in the table above. When a culture is likely to be needed, the **[Urinalysis, Complete Test with Reflex to Urine Culture](https://mitohealth.com/products/urinalysis-complete-with-reflex-to-culture)** runs a urine culture automatically if the urinalysis shows signs of a possible infection.


For the reference page on this finding, see[casts, crystals and mucus](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/casts-crystals-mucus) .


## When to get prompt care


**Contact your doctor if you have mucus in your urine along with symptoms of a UTI** \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]. **Contact them right away** if you have signs that an infection may have reached the kidneys \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \]:


- back or side pain;
- fever or chills;
- vomiting.


If you are pregnant, contact your prenatal clinician about urinary symptoms, and seek care promptly for fever or feeling ill \[[14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30895288/) \]\[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000521.htm) \].

## Frequently asked questions


### Is mucus in urine normal?


A small amount is normal. Mucus coats and moistens the urinary tract, and MedlinePlus describes a normal urinalysis as usually showing a small or moderate amount. A large amount may point to a urinary tract infection, a sexually transmitted infection, kidney stones or another condition, and usually leads to more tests to find the cause.


### What does mucus in urine mean for a female?


In women, mucus in a urine sample can come from the vagina or cervix rather than the bladder. Glands in the cervix and vaginal walls normally make mucus, and the amount rises around ovulation and in pregnancy. Many squamous epithelial cells on the same report point to this kind of contamination. A careful clean-catch repeat sample is the simplest way to tell. Mucus with urinary symptoms, or with positive nitrite or leukocyte esterase, is worth following up.


### Can a UTI cause mucus in urine?


Yes. A urinary tract infection is the first cause MedlinePlus lists for a large amount of mucus. Mucus alone does not diagnose an infection, though. The nitrite and leukocyte esterase results, the white blood cell and bacteria counts, and your symptoms carry more weight, and a urine culture confirms whether bacteria are growing.


### Can dehydration cause mucus in urine?


The sources reviewed for this article do not list dehydration as a cause of mucus in urine. Dehydration is a known reason for hyaline casts, a different finding on the same microscopic exam. Hyaline casts are made of the same kidney protein, uromodulin, that is abundant in normal urine, and they can appear in healthy people who are dehydrated.


### Is mucus in urine a sign of kidney problems?


Mucus on its own is not a kidney function test. The microscopic findings that point to the kidneys are casts, especially red or white blood cell casts, which form inside the kidney tubules. MedlinePlus does list kidney stones among the possible causes of a large amount of mucus.
